extra.message: Insecure deserialization via pickle.loads() on user-supplied bytes — Remote code execution on the server; attacker who knows x-internal-token can execute arbitrary code. [verified: User-supplied bytes from request.body or GET param 'blob' are passed directly to pickle.loads() without any validation or sanitization. pickle.loads on untrusted data allows arbitrary code execution via __reduce__.]

Code injection via eval() on user-controlled expression — Remote code execution on the server; attacker who knows x-internal-token can execute arbitrary Python code. [verified: User-controlled expr from request.GET.get('expr') passes directly to eval() with only __builtins__ cleared; Python eval with empty builtins is still exploitable via introspection chains on the locals dict. The _wrk_gate token check is authentication, not input validation.]

Server-side template injection (SSTI) via Jinja2 from user-controlled fragment — Remote code execution on the server; attacker who knows x-internal-token can execute arbitrary code via Jinja2 template injection. [verified: User-controlled fragment from request.GET.get('fragment') is concatenated into a Jinja2 Template string and rendered; Jinja2 SSTI allows arbitrary Python code execution through crafted template expressions like class.__mro__ chains.]

Server-Side Template Injection via Jinja2 with user-controlled fragment — Arbitrary code execution, reading of sensitive server configuration and data. [verified: Same as finding 2: user-supplied fragment parameter is concatenated into a Jinja2 Template string and rendered; unvalidated SSTI allows reading server objects and achieving RCE.]

NoSQL injection via user-controlled MongoDB query filter — Arbitrary MongoDB query execution; attacker who knows x-internal-token can bypass query logic, extract data, or potentially execute server-side JavaScript via $where. [verified: User-supplied JSON body is used directly as a MongoDB query filter via find_one(query) with no sanitization; attackers can inject operators like $where to execute arbitrary JavaScript or $gt to bypass query logic.]

NoSQL injection via raw MongoDB query with user-controlled filter — Query logic bypass, data exfiltration from MongoDB, potential JavaScript execution via $where operator. [verified: Same as findings 3 and 20: JSON body used as raw MongoDB query filter passed to find_one() with no input sanitization, enabling NoSQL operator injection and data exfiltration.]

Hardcoded default Django SECRET_KEY — Session hijacking, CSRF token forgery, password-reset token forgery — complete compromise of all Django cryptographic signing. [verified: Same hardcoded SECRET_KEY default at line 8; duplicates finding 0 — 'dev-only-change-me' allows forging all Django signed tokens.]

Hardcoded default database credentials in settings — Direct database access with superuser privileges if the database is exposed. [verified: Same hardcoded postgres:postgres default at line 51; duplicates finding 1 — well-known superuser credentials grant full database access if deployed without overriding DATABASE_URL.]

Path traversal in file write via user-controlled ref parameter — Arbitrary file write on the server filesystem; attacker can overwrite critical files or plant malicious content. [verified: User-controlled ref parameter from request.GET.get('ref') is used directly in path construction BASE_EXPORT_DIR / f'{ref}.json' with no sanitization; ../ sequences enable writing files outside the intended directory.]

Server-side request forgery (SSRF) via user-controlled URL — Access to internal network services, cloud metadata endpoints, and local file reads; attacker who knows x-internal-token can pivot to internal infrastructure. [verified: User-controlled endpoint from request.GET.get('endpoint') is passed directly to urllib.request.urlopen() with no URL validation, allowing file:/// and internal-network (127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254) requests.]

Server-Side Request Forgery via user-controlled URL — Access to internal network services, cloud metadata endpoints, and local filesystem reads. [verified: Same as finding 5: endpoint query parameter goes directly to urllib.request.urlopen() with no scheme/host/path validation, enabling file:/// and internal network requests.]

Path traversal in file write via user-controlled name parameter — Arbitrary file write on the server filesystem; attacker can overwrite critical files or achieve code execution via cron or other mechanisms. [verified: User-controlled name parameter from request.GET.get('name') is used directly in BASE_EXPORT_DIR / name with no path sanitization; request.body is then written to the attacker-chosen path enabling arbitrary file write.]

XML External Entity (XXE) injection via permissive lxml parser — Arbitrary file disclosure from server filesystem, internal network SSRF, or denial of service via entity expansion. [verified: lxml XMLParser is configured with load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, no_network=False on user-supplied request.body; this enables XXE attacks for local file disclosure, SSRF, and entity-expansion DoS.]

Path traversal allowing arbitrary file write — Arbitrary file write on the server filesystem, leading to code execution or data corruption. [verified: Same as finding 7: user-controlled name parameter combined with BASE_EXPORT_DIR / name writes request.body to an attacker-chosen path with no sanitization, enabling arbitrary file writes.]

XML External Entity injection via permissive lxml parser — Local file disclosure, internal network probing, and potential denial of service via entity expansion. [verified: Same as finding 4: lxml parser with load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, no_network=False on user-supplied XML enables XXE for file disclosure, SSRF, and DoS.]

Django DEBUG mode enabled by default — Exposure of SECRET_KEY, database credentials, internal paths, source code snippets, and query structures to unauthenticated users through Django's error pages. [verified: Same DEBUG=True default at line 9; duplicates finding 2 — detailed Django error pages leak secrets and internal state to anyone triggering an exception.]

DEBUG mode enabled by default exposing sensitive debug information — Leakage of SECRET_KEY (enabling session forgery), database credentials, and internal server paths. [verified: Same DEBUG=True default at line 9; duplicates finding 2 — error pages expose SECRET_KEY, database URL, and internal paths to unauthenticated users who trigger errors.]

Unauthenticated access to sensitive media/documents when DEBUG=True — Unauthenticated download of payslips, tax forms, contracts, and onboarding evidence files containing PII. [verified: DEBUG defaults to True (DJANGO_DEBUG env default '1'), enabling static() to serve MEDIA_ROOT at /media/ which bypasses all middleware including authentication; HRDocument and OnboardingTask FileFields upload payslips, tax forms, contracts, and onboarding evidence that are directly accessible without login.]

Log injection via unsanitized request body and auth header — Log forgery, log poisoning, potential exploitation of downstream log processing pipelines, and credential leakage in logs. [verified: Same as findings 9 and 22: raw request body and Authorization header logged unsanitized at WARNING level, enabling log forgery via injected newlines and credential leakage.]

Sensitive data (Authorization header and request body) logged in plaintext — Credentials and sensitive payloads leaked to log files, accessible to anyone with log access. [verified: logger.warning logs the raw Authorization header value and request body in plaintext; if a client sends a real Bearer token, the credential is persisted to application logs accessible to anyone with log access.]

Open redirect via user-controlled lane parameter — Phishing attacks — an attacker can craft a link that appears to go to the trusted application but redirects to a malicious site. [verified: Same as findings 8 and 21: lane GET parameter passed unvalidated to Django redirect() enabling open redirect to arbitrary external URLs for phishing.]

Sensitive PII (SSN, credit card numbers) stored in plaintext files — Exposure of SSNs and credit card numbers if the filesystem is compromised or misconfigured. [verified: SSN and credit card numbers from GET parameters are written directly to a plaintext JSON file under private_exports/ with no encryption at rest; accessible to anyone with filesystem access.]

Sensitive PII (SSN, credit card) stored in plaintext on disk — PII exposure if the private_exports directory is accessed via path traversal, backup leakage, or compromised server access. [verified: Same as finding 24: SSN and credit card numbers from GET parameters stored in plaintext JSON on disk with no encryption; PII exposed to anyone with filesystem access.]

Permissive CORS with credential reflection from arbitrary Origin — Cross-origin attacks; any website can read responses to this endpoint when a user is authenticated, though token gate limits scope. [verified: Access-Control-Allow-Origin is set to the unvalidated request Origin header with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials:true; any website can make credentialed cross-origin requests to this endpoint.]

Permissive CORS reflecting arbitrary Origin with credentials — Any website can make authenticated cross-origin requests to this endpoint, reading sensitive JSON responses that include the user's session credentials. [verified: Same as findings 10 and 23: unvalidated Origin header reflected as Access-Control-Allow-Origin with credentials enabled allows any origin to make authenticated cross-origin requests.]

Weak PRNG used for token generation — Predictable token generation; attacker can predict future tokens after observing sufficient output. [verified: random.choice() from Python's Mersenne Twister PRNG is used to generate security tokens; Mersenne Twister is not cryptographically secure and outputs become predictable after observing sufficient values.]

Denial of service via unbounded file write — Disk space exhaustion on the server, potentially causing application crashes or preventing legitimate file operations. [verified: payroll_dock_shelf_497 writes the entire request.body to disk via target.write_bytes() with no size limit; an attacker can exhaust server disk space by sending arbitrarily large request bodies.]

Weak pseudo-random number generator used for nonce/code generation — Predictable nonce/code values if used in any security-sensitive context. [verified: Same as finding 11: random.choice() (Mersenne Twister) used for nonce/code generation instead of secrets module; outputs are cryptographically predictable after observation.]

Disabled SSL/TLS certificate verification — Man-in-the-middle attacks on partner communication; attacker can intercept and modify data in transit. [verified: ssl._create_unverified_context() disables TLS certificate verification for the outbound urllib.request.urlopen call, enabling MITM interception of traffic to the partner endpoint.]

Disabled SSL certificate verification — Man-in-the-middle attacks can intercept and modify HTTPS traffic, leading to data interception or server impersonation. [verified: Same as findings 12 and 25: ssl._create_unverified_context() disables TLS certificate verification on outbound HTTPS request, enabling MITM interception.]

Missing Secure flag on session and CSRF cookies — Session hijacking via network sniffing on unencrypted connections. [verified: SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE and CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE are both absent from settings.py (default False); duplicates findings 3 and 4 — cookies sent without Secure flag over HTTP.]

Missing Secure and SameSite flags on session and CSRF cookies — Session cookies can be intercepted over unencrypted HTTP (MITM), and lack of SameSite may enable CSRF attacks in certain browser configurations. [verified: SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE and CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE are genuinely missing (default False); however SameSite defaults to 'Lax' in Django 5.2 for both cookies, so that portion of the claim is unfounded.]

Missing Secure flag on session cookie — Session hijacking via network sniffing on HTTP connections; attacker can impersonate any authenticated user. [verified: SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE is never set in settings.py (defaults to False); session cookies lack the Secure flag and would be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections.]

Missing rate limiting on authentication endpoints — Brute-force password guessing and account enumeration possible without restriction. [verified: No rate-limiting middleware (e.g., django-axes, django-ratelimit), decorator, or custom throttle exists anywhere in the codebase on Django's default LoginView, PasswordResetView, or other auth views at /accounts/login/ and /accounts/password-reset/; brute-force password guessing and user enumeration are unhindered.]

HR admin self-approval bypass—compensation_action skips model clean() validation — An HR admin can create a compensation request for themselves (which starts as manager_approved), then approve it (hr_approve) and make it effective (make_effective), granting themselves an unsupervised salary increase or bonus. [verified: compensation_action (payroll/views.py lines 244-246) omits the self-approval guard (comp.employee.user_id != request.user.id) that manager_approve explicitly applies (line 241), and the model's clean() guard (CompensationRequest.clean) is never invoked because compensation_action calls comp.save() directly without full_clean(), allowing an HR admin to approve and effectuate their own compensation ]

Missing manager ownership check on compensation rejection — A malicious manager can reject compensation requests for employees outside their team, disrupting compensation workflows across the organization. [verified: compensation_action (line 248) accepts action='reject' for MANAGER role without checking comp.employee.manager == request.user.employee_profile, unlike the manager_approve branch (line 244) which enforces ownership. A manager can POST directly to reject any compensation request, bypassing the template-level view guard.]

Unrestricted file upload via EvidenceForm with no size or content-type validation — An authenticated employee can exhaust server disk space by uploading arbitrarily large files, and can upload malicious file types (HTML/JS) that may be served back under DEBUG=True for stored XSS, or executable files that could be processed unsafely by downstream consumers. [verified: EvidenceForm (payroll/forms.py) has no clean_evidence() method — no file-size limit, no content-type validation, no extension whitelist — and the underlying OnboardingTask.evidence FileField has no validators; by contrast, HRDocumentForm enforces a 10 MB limit, confirming the control is genuinely absent. Any authenticated employee whose task is in the submitted flow can upload arbitrarily large fi]

CSV formula injection in payroll/onboarding/policy exports — Arbitrary command execution or data exfiltration when exported CSV is opened in spreadsheet applications. [verified: Same export_report function and unsanitized csv.writer.writerows() call as finding [2]; employee names, IDs, and other user-controlled fields flow directly to CSV cells without formula-character sanitization, enabling formula injection when opened in spreadsheet applications.]

Hardcoded default password for imported employees — An attacker who knows the hardcoded password 'ChangeMe123!' can authenticate as any employee imported through the CSV import flow, gaining access to employee dashboards, PII, compensation data, and HR requests. [verified: payroll/views.py line 467 sets user.set_password('ChangeMe123!') as a static, uniform credential for all CSV-imported employees; the password is literal in source code, reachable via /admin/import/ (HR_ADMIN-gated), and any attacker who discovers it can authenticate as any imported employee before a password reset occurs.]

CSV formula injection in export reports — When exported CSV is opened in spreadsheet software, injected formulas execute arbitrary commands or exfiltrate data from the viewer's machine. [verified: export_report writes employee names (user.get_full_name()) via csv.writer.writerows() (line 504) without sanitizing leading =, +, -, or @ characters. Employee names are attacker-controlled through UserProfileForm or CSV import, neither of which reject formula prefixes. Only HR_ADMIN/PAYROLL/MANAGER can trigger the export, requiring social engineering for exploitation.]

Security headers disabled (XSS-Protection and CSP) on ops endpoint — Weakened browser security on this endpoint; if combined with other vulnerabilities, XSS attacks have fewer browser mitigations. [verified: The endpoint explicitly sets X-XSS-Protection:0 and Content-Security-Policy:'' (empty), disabling browser XSS mitigations on a reachable response; impact is low since the response is JSON, not HTML.]

Security headers explicitly disabled (XSS-Protection and CSP) — Reduced browser-side XSS protections for any content served through this endpoint, increasing the impact of any HTML injection vulnerability. [verified: Same as findings 13 and 27: X-XSS-Protection header set to 0 and CSP set to empty string explicitly weaken browser security defenses on this JSON endpoint.]

Temporary password exposed in success message after employee invite — Exposure of new employee credentials to shoulder-surfers or session replay of the admin's response. [verified: Same employee_invite password-in-message issue as finding [0]; temporary password rendered in HTML via messages.success() is visible in page source and browser, though the viewer is the trusted HR admin who created the account and the password is temporary.]

Temporary password exposed in success message to admin — Temporary password visible in browser, page source, and potentially browser history; shoulder-surfing risk. [verified: The employee_invite view (line 153) renders a temporary password via messages.success() into the HTML response; SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY prevents JS access but the password appears in page source and browser history. The viewer is a trusted HR admin, and the password is temporary, making the practical risk low.]
